outcome: The unconditional Linnik constant remains L=5 (Xylouris, 2011, pre-window). A March 2026 preprint by Matías Bruna proves a new conditional bound on the least prime p in an arithmetic progression mod q, p ≪_ε q^{2+ε}, under the generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GLH) — a hypothesis strictly weaker than GRH — nearly matching the bound previously known only conditionally on GRH. No AI system was involved.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet 'Problems associated to Linnik's theorem' concerns the value of Linnik's constant L, the least exponent such that the least prime p(a,q) in an arithmetic progression a mod q satisfies p(a,q) ≪ q^L. As of the frozen revision (Jan 2024) the state was: unconditionally L=5 (Xylouris, 2011 PhD thesis, confirmed still current via the live Wikipedia article and multiple 2025-2026 secondary sources, e.g. arXiv:2511.05631), and conditionally on GRH, p(a,q) ≪ (φ(q)log q)^2, i.e. L=2+ε. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), I found no unconditional improvement to L=5 — it remains the record. I did find a genuine piece of progress: Matías Bruna's March 2026 preprint (arXiv:2603.25612, 'A conditional bound for the least prime in an arithmetic progression') proves p ≪_ε q^{2+ε} assuming only the generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GLH), which the paper's introduction explicitly states is weaker than GRH. This is new: it shows the strong GRH-conditional bound can be obtained from a weaker hypothesis, which is a real strengthening of the conditional landscape around this exact quantity (not a variant — it is literally the least-prime-in-AP function p(a,q) that the Wikipedia bullet is about). I read the HTML version of the paper directly (introduction and acknowledgements), which thanks only human collaborators (Asif Zaman, Andrew Granville, Université de Montréal) with no mention of any AI or computational tool. I also checked two adjacent but out-of-scope items that triage-adjacent searches surfaced: (1) Andrew Fiori's arXiv:2404.02329 (April 2024), a purely numerical/computational refinement of Wagstaff's 1979 conjectured bound 3φ(n)log(n)log(φ(n)), verified only up to 10^8 — this is a conjecture-refinement with numerical evidence, not a proof, and concerns a different (heuristic, average-case-flavored) quantity than Linnik's L, so it does not change this bullet's status by itself, though it is worth noting as adjacent computational work with no AI involved; (2) a 2024 Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal paper improving the least almost-prime (≤2 prime factors) bound from q^1.8345 to q^1.825 — this is about almost-primes, a genuinely different (relaxed) problem from the least-prime question in the bullet, so I classify it as a related/variant problem, not a case of this one. I found no AI system credited with any progress on Linnik's constant or the least-prime-in-AP problem in this window; a broad search for AI-assisted work in this specific area (least prime in AP) returned nothing relevant — the AI-and-mathematics hits that surfaced (Axiom Math's Lean proof of the 246 prime-gaps theorem, general AI-for-math surveys) are unrelated problems.
competing_reading: One could argue the Bruna result is 'beside the question' if one reads Linnik's constant narrowly as only the unconditional exponent — under that reading nothing at all has happened in-window and status would be 'open' with no_change_found true. I reject this narrow reading because the Wikipedia bullet and its own article explicitly discuss both the unconditional record and the GRH-conditional bound as part of 'problems associated to Linnik's theorem,' so a new, weaker-hypothesis derivation of essentially the same conditional bound is squarely in scope as progress on the conditional side of the same quantity, even though the unconditional constant L did not move.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g. via a later expert citation, a survey update, or citations to Bruna's paper) that the GLH-conditional bound is accepted as correct and non-trivial relative to prior conditional results, and whether any subsequent work improves the unconditional L=5 record within the window.

dead_ends: Initial WebFetch of the Bruna PDF (raw, non-HTML) returned an inconsistent hypothesis name ('Generalized Linnik Hypothesis') that conflicted with three later, consistent extractions ('generalized Lindelöf hypothesis'); resolved by re-fetching the HTML version, which gave a stable, internally consistent reading and is the version relied on here.

A machine-learning-guided search for 28-term prime arithmetic progressions (a different problem, PAP-k records) surfaced in AI+math searches but is unrelated to the least-prime-in-AP / Linnik constant question and was excluded.
The 2024 almost-prime bound improvement (q^1.8345 to q^1.825) was checked and excluded as a variant problem (almost-primes, not primes).

incomplete: I did not access the almost-prime paper (link.springer.com/article/10.21136/CMJ.2024.0459-23) directly — its content is taken from a search snippet only, but it was excluded from scope anyway so this does not affect the status determination. I also did not exhaustively check for citations to the Bruna preprint or any expert digestion of it beyond the paper itself, since as a March 2026 preprint it is unlikely to have been formally reviewed yet; this is reflected in the 'progress' status (not 'resolved' or 'claimed', since it is progress on a conditional bound for a problem that remains open) and medium confidence.
